query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a cryogenic rolling treatment followed by a low‐temperature annealing process to a cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) will refine its lamellar microstructure and induce coherent nano‐scale precipitates that simultaneously improve strength and ductility relative to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase (e.g., FCC + BCC or soft + hard phase) lamellar microstructure
generation.intervention: Cryogenic rolling (to impose high strain at low temperature) followed by a tailored low-temperature annealing step
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed under controlled cryogenic rolling conditions and annealed at a temperature low enough to initiate fine-scale precipitation without coarsening (e.g., below typical recrystallization temperatures) and then tested at room temperature under quasi-static loading
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, ultrafine-grained duplex lamellar structure with coherent nano-scale (e.g., L12) precipitates embedded within the ductile matrix
generation.mechanism: The cryogenic rolling creates a high density of dislocations and refines the lamellar spacing, while subsequent annealing allows controlled precipitation of coherent particles. These precipitates act as effective dislocation pins and promote a two-hierarchical constraint effect, maintaining high work hardening without early crack propagation. Together, these changes lead to simultaneous improvements in yield strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to show an increase in yield strength (on the order of >20% improvement compared to the as-cast condition) and a maintained or slightly enhanced elongation (ductility) relative to the baseline eutectic HEA.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy state (e.g., the reported performance of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 with ~944 MPa strength and ~25.6% ductility) and conventionally processed (non-cryogenic rolled) samples
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected provided that the rolling reduction and annealing temperature/time are optimized to avoid over-coarsening of precipitates or recrystallization that might otherwise negate the twin benefits. Deviations from these processing windows may not yield the improved strength–ductility synergy.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements depend on the specific alloy composition and processing parameters. There is uncertainty regarding the optimal annealing conditions to balance precipitate size and distribution without inducing excessive residual stresses or over-recovery.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of a eutectic HEA (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1): one set following conventional processing (as-cast or room-temperature deformation) and a second set undergoing cryogenic rolling followed by a low-temperature annealing treatment optimized for fine-scale precipitation. Characterize the microstructure with SEM/TEM to verify lamellar refinement and precipitate development, and perform room-temperature tensile tests to assess yield strength, elongation, and work hardening behavior.
measurements: Grain/lamellar spacing and precipitate morphology (via TEM/SEM)
Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryogenic rolling and annealing treatment does not result in a statistically significant increase in yield strength (e.g., >20% improvement) along with maintained or improved ductility and associated work hardening compared to the conventionally processed samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al. [,] designed the CoCrFeNiNbx EHEAs and found that the microstructures were stable from 600 °C to 900 °C.
